name: Hana Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I get to Brandt's Garage at half seven, it's a little two-bay place behind the bakery on Mill Lane, and Walter, the owner, has the kettle on before I'm in. Most of my day is brakes, suspension, oil services and exhausts on older cars, the ten- and fifteen-year-old hatchbacks people keep running. I like the feel of a seized bolt finally giving, honestly. What wears me out is the electrical stuff, because I'm still slow at it and Walter has to bail me out more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spent four years at a parcel depot after school, scanning boxes on nights, and I hated every minute. I saved most of what I earned because I was living with my gran, and when she died she left me a share of her flat, so I've got a proper cushion. I retrained at twenty-four and Walter took me on. I'm two years in and still the junior, but the pay is good for a place this size because Walter can't find anyone else who'll stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that I told you so. Every year someone comes in waving a new gadget and every year the cars still need someone under them with a breaker bar. I'd probably post something smug in the group chat with the lads from college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I'm not good with the new tech and I know it, so a world where it fizzles out suits me down to the ground. My job stays my job, my pay stays decent, and I get more time to catch up on the electrics without some app making me look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing, and I'd finally book the evening course on auto electrics at the college that I keep putting off. It's about four hundred for the term and I can pay that out of savings without thinking. Maybe I'd ask Walter for a bit more responsibility on the inspection days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like the floor stays where it is. I've got my savings, I've got a boss who needs me, and there are three other garages on the ring road that would take me tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine tasks it takes over could touch some jobs. Is there anything in your day that's routine screen work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, which is part of why I'm calm. Walter does the invoices on an old laptop and orders parts by phone from the factors, the parts suppliers. If a bit of software does his ordering faster, fine, that's his side of the counter, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work, if anyone, would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter, a bit, because he's sixty-three and his back is going. In this picture nothing changes, so the real question is still who takes over when he stops. That's the worry I already have, AI or no AI.

say: I'd tell people the **hype** fizzled, like every other gadget that was meant to change garages.
I'd post something **smug** in the college group chat about cars still needing hands.
think: Privately it's a **relief**, because I'm slow with new tech and this world doesn't punish that.
My real worry stays the same: **who takes over** the garage when the owner retires.
do: Book the **auto electrics** evening course, about four hundred for the term, paid from savings.
Ask the owner for **more responsibility** on inspection days within the year.
feel: Mostly **calm**, like the floor stays exactly where it is.
A small **nag** about the owner's bad back and who runs the place next.
S0.quote: Every year someone comes in waving a new gadget and every year the cars still need someone under them with a breaker bar.
fieldNote: Her **security** rests on savings, a short-handed boss and three rival garages nearby.
She admits she is **slow with electrics** and is glad nothing forces her to catch up fast.
The only pre-existing worry is **succession**: the owner is sixty-three and has a bad back.

steps.text: Keep doing brakes, suspension and servicing at the same two-bay garage
Take the college evening course in auto electrics this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's the bosses and the tech firms getting richer again while the rest of us adapt. Online I'd share stuff about the motor trade union pushing for training paid by employers, not by us. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. The thinking bits of my job are exactly where I'm weak: reading fault codes, working out what's wrong before the spanners come out. If a tablet does the diagnosis, then the junior who can only do the hands-on part is worth less, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, not just say I support it, that's twenty a month. I'd push myself through the electrics course and maybe the hybrid safety certificate. I hate the idea, but I'd probably have to let Walter show me the diagnostic tablet instead of handing it back to him every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's still there, the cars still need fixing, but the ground's shifting under the bit of the job I'm worst at. It's like the gearbox is fine but there's a noise you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. If Walter bought a diagnostic system that talks you through faults, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it because I'd have to, not because I'd want to. I'd probably double-check everything it said with a meter, which would make me slower, not faster. I know that's stubborn, but I don't trust what I can't see inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies selling it, and the governments that let them roll it out with no plan for workers. Nobody asked me, a mechanic in a two-bay garage, whether I wanted my job split in half. If there's no rule that the boss pays for retraining, it falls on people like me.

say: I'd say **bosses and tech firms** get richer while workers do all the adapting.
I'd share posts backing the **union's push** for employer-paid retraining for mechanics.
think: Diagnosis is the **thinking part** of the job, and it's exactly where I'm weakest.
If a tablet diagnoses, a junior who only turns spanners is **worth less**.
do: Join the **motor trade union** properly, paying about twenty a month.
Finish the electrics course and add the **hybrid safety** certificate within the year.
Let the owner train her on the **diagnostic tablet**, however reluctantly.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a noise in the gearbox you can't quite place.
Some **resentment** that nobody asked workers before splitting the job.
S1.quote: Nobody asked me, a mechanic in a two-bay garage, whether I wanted my job split in half.
fieldNote: Her public line is **political anger**; her private fear is about her own weak diagnostic skills.
She would use the tool only **under pressure** and would double-check it, making her slower.
Blames **tech firms and government** for rolling change out without a worker plan.

steps.text: Join the motor trade union and pay the monthly dues
Finish the electrics course and take the hybrid safety certificate
Learn the garage's diagnostic tablet with the owner, step by step

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we were warned about, and that governments need to step in now, not after. I'd be at whatever protest the union organised. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that you can't let a few companies decide this for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in this trade by about 2031. The diagnosis goes in 2028, and then three years later a robot can do the brake job I'm good at. I'm twenty-seven now. I'll have spent seven years learning a trade that disappears before I'm even thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big and keep my savings where they are. I'd go to every union meeting. I'd stay at Brandt's as long as Walter keeps the doors open, because three years of good wages is three years of savings. Then I'd look hard at work where people want a person in the room, like care work, even though I can't picture myself doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I left a job I hated to find one I liked, and now I'd be back at the start. The money means I won't be on the street, but that's not the same as being all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got more than six months saved and a share of a flat. Does that change how this feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I eat, not whether I sleep. My gran's money buys me time to retrain, maybe two years if I'm careful. But time to retrain into what? That's the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Walter, the week it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm staying as long as he wants me, and I'd mean it. Then I'd probably ask him straight out whether he's planning to sell. He'd tell me the truth, he always does, and I think I already know he'd sell.

say: I'd say **governments must step in** now, before companies decide everything for everyone.
I'd turn up to any **union protest** organised against fast job losses.
think: I expect to be **finished in the trade** by about 2031, when robots arrive.
Seven years spent learning a trade that **disappears** before I'm thirty-two.
do: Freeze **big spending** and keep the savings untouched as a two-year retraining fund.
Stay at the garage for the **three paid years** before robots arrive.
Research **care work** and other jobs where people want a person present.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of starting over after finally finding work she liked.
**Safe from hardship**, but not from sleepless nights about what comes next.
S2.quote: I'll have spent seven years learning a trade that disappears before I'm even thirty-two.
fieldNote: The three-year robot gap is **breathing room** for savings, not safety for her career.
Savings change **whether she eats**, not whether she sleeps, in her own words.
Strong loyalty to the owner; she expects he would **sell the garage**.

steps.text: Go to every union meeting and protest about the job losses
Freeze big purchases and keep the inheritance money untouched
Visit the job centre to ask about care work and similar jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that the government's got five years to sort out training and income for people like us, and no excuse. I'd be pushing the union to make it the only issue. Online I'd be the annoying one sharing petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years feels like a bit more than a breath. The diagnosis side goes by 2031 and the hands-on side by 2034, so I'd have seven years of decent pay. I'd be thirty-four. That's young enough to start again, but I hate that I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into savings, maybe an extra two hundred a month, since I'd know the clock was running. I'd stop the hybrid course halfway, because why get better at a trade with a date on it? I'd volunteer at the community centre's repair café on Saturdays to see whether teaching people to fix things is something I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less of a punch than the two-year one, more of a slow ache. Every brake job and every oil service I do, I'd be quietly counting down the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop the hybrid course. A minute ago you said diagnostics was where you needed to improve. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, that's a contradiction. I suppose in the slow version I'd keep at it, and in this one I'd drop it, because it's money and evenings spent on something with a sell-by date. I'd rather put the evenings into something with a future, even if I don't know what that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Priya from college, who's a bus fitter for the council. Council jobs move slow, and she'd probably tell me to get in there while I can. I'd listen to her more than to anyone online.

say: I'd say the government has **five years** to sort out training and income support.
I'd push the union to make this its **only campaign**, and share petitions online.
think: Five years means **seven years** of decent pay before robots arrive in 2034.
At thirty-four I'm **young enough** to start again, though I hate having to.
do: Save an extra **two hundred** a month, knowing the clock is running.
Drop the hybrid course and spend evenings testing **other work** instead.
Volunteer Saturdays at the **repair café** to see if teaching suits her.
feel: **Anxious**, a slow ache rather than a punch, counting down every service.
S3.quote: Every brake job and every oil service I do, I'd be quietly counting down the years.
fieldNote: With five years warning she **stops investing** in the trade itself, a sharp shift.
Named the contradiction honestly and **chose a future** over improving at mechanics.
Trusts a **friend in council work** more than anything she reads online.

steps.text: Put an extra two hundred a month into savings
Ask a friend about bus fitter jobs at the council depot
Push the union branch to make job losses its main campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for a mess. I'd want rules on how fast garages can bring robots in, and a fund for retraining. I'd say it at union meetings and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years plus three for the robots is a long time. I'd be forty by 2039. I think I'd stay a mechanic most of that, get properly good at it, and then move into something nearby, maybe teaching at the college, before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Brandt's and finish the electrics and hybrid courses after all, because ten years is worth investing in. I'd keep saving like I do now. Around year five I'd start asking the college about assessor or tutor work, since someone has to teach the last mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's like knowing your car will need a new clutch in two years. Annoying, but you can plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your gran have said about all this, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have said learn to cook and keep your money in a tin, which is basically what I do anyway. She lived through a factory closing in her twenties and still owned a flat by fifty. She'd say ten years is a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with your money in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably buy a small place of my own with my savings and my share of the flat, since I'd still have steady wages for years to get a mortgage. A home is the one thing a robot can't take off you, so I'd want my own place sorted by thirty-five.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for a messy, unfair rollout.
I'd call for **rules on robot speed** in garages and a retraining fund.
think: I'd be **forty** by 2039, so I could stay a mechanic most of that time.
Near the end I'd move into **teaching mechanics** at the college.
do: Finish both the **electrics and hybrid** courses, since ten years is worth it.
Buy a **small home** with savings and the flat share by thirty-five.
Ask the college about **tutor or assessor** work around year five.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, like a clutch you know is going.
S4.quote: A home is the one thing a robot can't take off you, so I'd want my own place sorted by thirty-five.
fieldNote: With a decade she **invests back** into her trade, unlike in the five-year picture.
Her late gran's **thrift and history** shape how she thinks about risk.
Buying a **home** is her defence against change she can't control.

steps.text: Finish the auto electrics and hybrid safety courses at the college
Buy a small flat using savings and the share of the old flat
Stay on at the two-bay garage for most of the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is a guarantee that the boss or the government pays your wage while you retrain, not some voucher for an online course. And a union that's actually in the room when the decisions get made.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot doing the job even if it was safe. I wouldn't. People bring their cars to a small garage because they trust the person behind the counter, and that matters more than anyone in an office thinks. Walter's customers have been coming for thirty years.

headlineQuote: People bring their cars to a small garage because they trust the person behind the counter, and that matters more than anyone in an office thinks.
portrait: Hana is a **junior mechanic** at a two-bay garage, retrained after four years on depot night shifts.
She has **strong savings** and a share of her late gran's flat, but is slow with electrics.
She never uses AI and **distrusts** any tool she can't see inside.
Her mood climbs from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
She **blames tech firms** and government and turns to the union for answers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose the trade by thirty-one with nowhere obvious to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid wage while retraining**, covered by the employer or the government, not a course voucher.
A **union in the room** when decisions about robots and jobs get made.
